title: Pennsylvania Measles Outbreak Spreads to Snyder County After Lowe's Exposure
excerpt: A Snyder County resident has tested positive for measles, with potential exposure at a Selinsgrove Lowe's store. The case marks further geographic spread of Pennsylvania's worst measles outbreak in decades.
body:
• A Snyder County, Pennsylvania resident has tested positive for measles and may have exposed others at a Lowe's store in Selinsgrove
  • The case extends Pennsylvania's measles outbreak beyond the Lancaster-Lebanon epicenter, with over 100 confirmed cases statewide in 2026
  • Health officials urge unvaccinated individuals to check their MMR vaccination status and contact providers if symptoms develop

A resident of Snyder County in central Pennsylvania has tested positive for measles, potentially exposing shoppers at a Lowe's home improvement store in Selinsgrove, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health. The department issued a public alert on July 22, warning unvaccinated individuals who visited the store to monitor for symptoms and contact their healthcare providers.

The Snyder County case represents a significant geographic expansion of Pennsylvania's ongoing measles outbreak, which has been concentrated in the Lancaster and Lebanon county areas since it began in late April. Snyder County sits roughly 80 miles north of Lancaster, raising concerns that the virus is reaching new communities across the state.

A Growing Statewide Crisis

As of early July 2026, the Pennsylvania Department of Health had confirmed more than 100 measles cases across the state — already exceeding the full-year 2025 total by more than five times, according to Medical Daily. The outbreak, which the department says involves exclusively unvaccinated individuals or those with unknown vaccination status, has now touched at least eight counties, including Lancaster, Lebanon, York, Northumberland, Berks, Dauphin, Chester, and now Snyder.

"Our epidemiologists, our community health nurses, and our local partners are working diligently to get measles under control."

— Dr. Debra Bogen, Pennsylvania Secretary of Health

Nationally, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 2,170 confirmed measles cases across 41 jurisdictions as of July 2 — putting the U.S. within striking distance of the full-year 2025 total of 2,289 cases, the highest annual count since 1991. Among 2026 cases, 93 percent occurred in unvaccinated individuals, and 138 people — roughly 6 percent — have been hospitalized.

What Happened in Snyder County

The Pennsylvania Department of Health confirmed a Snyder County resident tested positive for measles and may have exposed others at a Lowe's store in Selinsgrove, according to the Snyder County government and multiple local news outlets including WNEP, PennLive, and WKOK. Health officials are conducting contact tracing and urging anyone who visited the store during the exposure window to monitor for symptoms for up to 21 days.

Measles is one of the most contagious infectious diseases known. Up to nine out of ten unvaccinated people who come in close contact with an infected person will develop the disease. The virus can remain infectious in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area, making exposure possible even without direct contact.

Symptoms to watch for include high fever, dry cough, runny nose, red and watery eyes, and a distinctive red rash that starts on the face and spreads downward. Symptoms typically appear 10 to 14 days after exposure but can take up to 21 days.

Declining Vaccination Rates Fuel the Outbreak

The outbreak reflects a broader national trend of declining MMR vaccination coverage. According to Drug Topics, national MMR coverage among kindergartners fell from 95.2 percent in the 2019-2020 school year to 92.5 percent in 2024-2025 — dropping below the 95 percent threshold scientists consider necessary to maintain community immunity. The CDC estimates this left approximately 286,000 kindergartners unprotected in the most recent school year.

Pennsylvania's vaccination rates tell a similar story. While nearly 94 percent of the state's kindergartners received both required doses of the MMR vaccine during the 2024-2025 school year, pockets of low coverage exist across many counties. In Lancaster County, the outbreak epicenter, the kindergarten vaccination rate is approximately 88.5 percent — well below the herd immunity threshold.

"The best protection against measles is to get vaccinated. With two measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine doses, you are at extremely low risk of getting measles and spreading it to your family and community."

— Dr. Debra Bogen, Pennsylvania Secretary of Health

What Indian Americans in Pennsylvania Should Know

Pennsylvania is home to a substantial Indian American population, particularly in the Philadelphia suburbs and central Pennsylvania corridors. With the outbreak now spanning multiple counties from Lancaster to Snyder, health officials are urging all residents — including those who may have received childhood vaccinations in India — to verify their MMR vaccination records.

Adults who received only one MMR dose, or who are uncertain of their vaccination history, should consult a healthcare provider. There is no harm in receiving an additional dose if records are unavailable. Families planning travel between the U.S. and India should ensure that all members, including infants, are up to date on their vaccinations.

What Comes Next

The Pennsylvania Department of Health has administered more than 1,300 MMR vaccine doses statewide in 2026, including over 430 through pop-up clinics in the Lancaster-Lebanon region. The state has also recommended early MMR vaccination for infants starting at six months of age in affected counties, lowering the standard threshold of 12 to 15 months.

Governor Josh Shapiro's administration launched a public measles dashboard on July 14 to keep parents and the public informed of ongoing cases. Health officials warn that if the United States records more than 365 days of continuous endemic transmission before the end of 2026, the country could lose its measles elimination status — a milestone it achieved in 2000.

Anyone who believes they may have been exposed to measles should contact their healthcare provider or call the Pennsylvania Department of Health's toll-free hotline at 877-PA-HEALTH (877-724-3258). Officials stress that callers should phone ahead before visiting any medical facility to prevent further spread.
